body_html:
On November 17, two of technology's most recognizable founders put Malibu addresses on the market within days of each other. Canyon News reports that former Google CEO Eric Schmidt listed his Malibu Colony beach house for $37.5 million, while Google co-founder Sergey Brin listed his Point Dume property at 29060 Cliffside Drive for $33.5 million. Together, that is roughly $71 million in trophy coastal inventory arriving in a single week — and, more interestingly for anyone reading the design of this coastline, it places Malibu's two signature lot typologies side by side on the same tape.

What does $71 million buy in Malibu in 2026?

At this level, you are not buying square footage — you are buying a relationship to the Pacific. Schmidt's $37.5 million listing sits in Malibu Colony, the gated, sand-level row where lots are famously narrow and the house meets the water with almost no setback. Brin's $33.5 million Point Dume parcel is the opposite condition: elevated bluff, wider footprint, ocean read from height.

These are two different architectural problems. The Colony rewards horizontal compression and light brought in from the sides; Point Dume rewards the freestanding volume and the long view. Both listings, per Canyon News, come to market in the same November window.

Why are two founders listing in the same week?

The honest answer is that at the very top of the Malibu market, timing is personal, not macro — portfolio rebalancing, a move, a change of use. But the signal still matters. When $71 million of inventory from name-recognition owners surfaces at once, it refreshes the comparable set that every subsequent Malibu appraisal and listing is measured against.

It also exposes something about how this market values homes. In both cases the narrative is overwhelmingly about location and provenance — the address, the beach, the view. The building itself is treated as a near-neutral vessel that a buyer will likely reconfigure or replace.

On this coast, land is priced for permanence and the house is priced as if it were temporary. That gap is the whole story.

That is the structural inefficiency hiding inside a headline about two founders. The parcel is underwritten for the long term; the structure, in most trophy transactions, is underwritten as disposable. On a coastline that faces both wildfire exposure inland and corrosive salt air at the shore, that is a strange thing to accept at $30-plus million.

What does this mean for the LA luxury market?

For the Westside market, the read is continuity. Malibu's absolute ceiling remains intact: parcels like these still clear in the mid-to-high eight figures, and the buyer pool that competes for sand-level Colony or bluff-top Point Dume is unbothered by the broader rate environment. New inventory at this tier tends to set the frame rather than test it.

The subtler shift is in what sophisticated buyers increasingly scrutinize. As insurability has become the binding constraint on California coastal ownership, the question of how a house is actually built — its envelope, its roof assembly, its resilience to the next cycle — is migrating from an afterthought to a line item in the valuation. A trophy lot with a combustible, aging structure now carries a quiet discount that a resilient one does not. In 2026, construction is becoming part of the comp, not just the land.

Expect the pattern to continue: Malibu's premier typologies will keep trading on provenance and view, but the gap between a parcel's permanence and a structure's fragility will keep widening. The founders listing this week are selling the land's story. The next generation of Malibu value will increasingly be written in the building.
